pos: n. (an ascetic who lived on top of a pillar, chiefly in fifth- and sixth-century Syria)
etymology: Greek stulos, a pillar, with the suffix -ites, one belonging to; a pillar-dweller.
biblical_def: A stylite was an ascetic who lived on the platform of a pillar. Simeon the Elder, who began about 423 and ended on a column some fifty feet high outside Antioch, was the first and most famous, and he had imitators across Syria for two centuries. The motive was partly flight from crowds that would not leave him alone, and partly a deliberate spectacle of renunciation; pilgrims came in thousands, and Simeon preached, arbitrated disputes and converted many from his pillar. A Protestant assessment has to be candid in both directions. Scripture knows of men driven to extremity by faith — “they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth” (Heb 11:38) — and does not sneer at them. But a pillar is not a cave; it is a platform, visible for miles, and visibility is the one thing Christ excluded from devotion: “they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast” (Mat 6:16). The pillar's very name is an irony, since Scripture gives the word to the church and to the men who hold her up — “James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars” (Gal 2:9) — not to a man who climbs one.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stylite as a kind of monk who lived on the tops of pillars, also called a pillarist; pillar as a kind of irregular column; and ascetic as one who retires from the customary business of life and devotes himself to exercises of piety.
webster_full: STYLITE, n. A monk who lived on the top of a pillar; a pillarist.
PILLAR, n. A kind of irregular column, round and insulated, but deviating from the proportions of a just column; a supporter; that which sustains or upholds.
ASCETIC, n. One who retires from the customary business of life, and devotes himself to the duties of piety and devotion; a hermit; a recluse.
AUSTERE, a. Severe; harsh; rigid; stern; applied to persons and to their manners and discipline.
SPECTACLE, n. A show; a gazing stock; something exhibited to view as extraordinary, or something that is beheld as unusual.
scriptures: (Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
Mat 6:16
Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.
Gal 2:9

And when James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given unto me, they gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship; that we should go unto the heathen, and they unto the circumcision.
Col 2:23
Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.
corruption_summary: The pillar ascetic: real endurance made into a public exhibition, which is the one thing Christ forbade in devotion.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the spectacle, and Paul had already classified it. Self-chosen severity that draws a crowd he calls “a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body” (Col 2:23) — the word shew doing the work. A devotion arranged to be seen has its reward in the seeing, which is exactly Christ's verdict on the disfigured faces: “Verily I say unto you, They have their reward” (Mat 6:16).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that endurance is sometimes required of a Christian and never to be arranged by him. “For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things” (1Ti 4:8) sets the proportion: the body may be disciplined, but it is not the ladder, and fifty feet of masonry brings no man nearer God than the ground does.
roots_summary: Greek stulos (G4769), a pillar; Greek askesis, training; Greek theatron (G2302), a spectacle; Greek eremos (G2048), a desert; Hebrew ammud (H5982), a pillar.
roots_lines: Greek stulos (G4769) — a pillar; “will I make a pillar in the temple of my God” (Rev 3:12) — a promise, not a practice.
Hebrew ammud (H5982) — a pillar or column; the pillar of cloud and of fire, God's own and not a man's platform.
Greek eremos (G2048) — desert, a lonely place; the Syrian ascetics' proper setting.
Greek theatron (G2302) — a theatre, a spectacle; Paul uses it of apostolic shame, never of chosen display.
Greek egkrateia (G1466) — self-control; a fruit of the Spirit, and the thing a pillar cannot manufacture.
usage: “Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38) — Scripture's respect for the driven-out, which is not the same as the self-exhibited.
“who seemed to be pillars” (Gal 2:9) — the biblical use of the word, given to men who held up a church.
“For bodily exercise profiteth little” (1Ti 4:8) — the measure of every austerity.

pos: n. (a woman enclosed for life in a cell, usually attached to a church, for prayer and counsel)
etymology: Greek anachoreo, to withdraw, through Latin anachoreta; the feminine of anchorite, with the English suffix -ess.
biblical_def: An anchoress was a woman walled into a cell — often a small room built against the wall of a parish church, with a squint through which she could see the altar and a window onto the street through which she gave counsel. The rite of enclosure was a burial service. England had more anchoresses than anchorites, and the Ancrene Wisse was written to guide them; Julian of Norwich is the best known. The vocation was not idleness: these women prayed, copied, taught, and advised a steady traffic of ordinary people at the window, so that an anchoress was often the most accessible spiritual counsellor in a town. Scripture commends neither the enclosure nor its denial in those terms, but it does locate a woman's calling in relationships rather than in isolation, and it gives older women a teaching office exercised among the living: “That they may teach the young women to be sober, to love their husbands, to love their children” (Tit 2:4). A cell cannot do that work. What the anchoress's window attempted — wisdom given to whoever came — Scripture asks of a household and a congregation, in the open.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines anchoress or ancress as a female anchoret; anchoret as a hermit, one who retires from society into a desert or solitary place to avoid the temptations of the world; and recluse as shut up, retired from the world.
webster_full: ANCHORESS, n. A female anchoret; a woman who retires from the world for religious devotion.
ANCHORET, ANCHORITE, n. A hermit; a recluse; one who retires from society into a desert or solitary place, to avoid the temptations of the world and devote himself to religious duties.
RECLUSE, a. Shut up; sequestered; retired from the world or from public notice; solitary.
CELL, n. A very small and close apartment, as in a prison or a monastery; the hut of a hermit.
ENCLOSE, v.t. To surround; to shut up; to encompass; to confine on all sides.
scriptures: Tit 2:4
That they may teach the young women to be sober, to love their husbands, to love their children,
Tit 2:5
To be discreet, chaste, keepers at home, good, obedient to their own husbands, that the word of God be not blasphemed.
She stretcheth out her hand to the poor; yea, she reacheth forth her hands to the needy.

Well reported of for good works; if she have brought up children, if she have lodged strangers, if she have washed the saints' feet, if she have relieved the afflicted, if she have diligently followed every good work.
corruption_summary: A woman enclosed for life: real prayer and real counsel at the window, in a vocation that walled her away from the relationships Scripture gives her.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a godly woman's wisdom is meant to circulate among the living. “She stretcheth out her hand to the poor; yea, she reacheth forth her hands to the needy” (Pro 31:20) and “if she have lodged strangers, if she have washed the saints' feet, if she have relieved the afflicted” (1Ti 5:10) describe hands that reach and feet that go, neither of which a cell permits.

The historic error was to treat enclosure as the higher path for a devout woman, so that the serious option was a wall. Scripture's own charge is domestic, public and unglamorous: “To be discreet, chaste, keepers at home, good, obedient to their own husbands, that the word of God be not blasphemed” (Tit 2:5). That is a calling, not a consolation prize, and the medieval church did its daughters no favours by implying otherwise.
roots_summary: Greek anachoreo (G402), to withdraw; Greek monos (G3441), alone; Hebrew badad (H909), to be isolated; Greek hesuchia (G2271), quietness; Hebrew chokmah (H2451), wisdom.
roots_lines: Greek anachoreo (G402) — to withdraw, to depart; used of Christ withdrawing to pray, always temporarily.
Greek monos (G3441) — alone, solitary; the root also of monk.
Hebrew badad (H909) — to be separate or isolated; in Scripture usually a condition of grief.
Greek hesuchia (G2271) — quietness, stillness; a quality commended, and attainable without a wall.
Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom; “She stretcheth out her hand to the poor” (Pro 31:20) shows where it goes.
usage: “That they may teach the young women to be sober” (Tit 2:4) — a teaching office exercised among the living.
“if she have washed the saints' feet” (1Ti 5:10) — mercy that requires proximity.
“she reacheth forth her hands to the needy” (Pro 31:20) — hands a cell cannot reach with.

pos: n. (the dwelling of a hermit; a cell or small house in a solitary place)
etymology: Greek eremos, desert or lonely, through Latin eremita, a desert-dweller, and Old French hermitage; the desert-dweller's house.
biblical_def: A hermitage is a hermit's dwelling: a cell, a hut, sometimes a cave, set apart in a wood, on a cliff or in a fen. Medieval England was full of them, and they were not all occupied by contemplatives — many a hermit kept a bridge, a ferry or a lighthouse and lived on alms for the service. Scripture furnishes the pattern it was built on. Elijah lodged in a cave and heard God there: “And he came thither unto a cave, and lodged there; and, behold, the word of the LORD came to him” (1Ki 19:9). John grew up in the deserts, “And the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, and was in the deserts till the day of his shewing unto Israel” (Luk 1:80). The Lord himself sought solitary places to pray. What Scripture never does is make the dwelling permanent or meritorious. Elijah's cave was a station on a journey and God's question there was a rebuke — “What doest thou here, Elijah?” (1Ki 19:9). John came out of the desert to preach. The hermitage is a legitimate retreat and a poor address: withdrawal in Scripture is always for the sake of a return.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hermitage as the habitation of a hermit, a cell or dwelling in a solitary place; hermit as a person who retires from society and lives in solitude; and solitude as loneliness, a lonely life, remoteness from society.
webster_full: HERMITAGE, n. The habitation of a hermit; a house or hut with its appendages, in which a hermit dwells.
HERMIT, n. A person who retires from society and lives in solitude; a recluse; an anchoret.
HERMITICAL, a. Pertaining to a hermit, or to retired life.
SOLITUDE, n. Loneliness; a state of being alone; a lonely life; also, a lonely place; a desert.
CAVE, n. A hollow place in the earth; a subterraneous cavern; a den.
scriptures: And he came thither unto a cave, and lodged there; and, behold, the word of the LORD came to him, and he said unto him, What doest thou here, Elijah?
Luk 1:80
And the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, and was in the deserts till the day of his shewing unto Israel.
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
Mar 1:35
And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed.
corruption_summary: The hermit's dwelling: withdrawal is biblical as a station and not as an address, since every scriptural retreat is for the sake of a return.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the rhythm rather than the residence. “he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed” (Mar 1:35) is followed in the next verses by his going to the towns to preach; the withdrawal served the mission and did not replace it.

The live error, then and now, is to mistake escape for devotion. Elijah's cave is the test case, because he had real cause for flight and God still asked him “What doest thou here, Elijah?” (1Ki 19:9) and sent him back with three commissions. A Christian wearied of men may need a quiet place; he does not need a permanent one, and Scripture declines to make solitude a vocation.
roots_summary: Greek eremos (G2048), desert; Greek eremia (G2047), a wilderness; Hebrew midbar (H4057), wilderness; Hebrew mearah (H4631), a cave; Greek anachoreo (G402), to withdraw.
roots_lines: Greek eremos (G2048) — desert, lonely, deserted; the root of both hermit and eremite.
Hebrew midbar (H4057) — wilderness, pasture land beyond the settlements; “The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness” (Isa 40:3).
Hebrew mearah (H4631) — a cave; Elijah's lodging, and David's.
Greek anachoreo (G402) — to withdraw; the verb of a temporary retreat.
Greek eremia (G2047) — a desert place; “they wandered in deserts, and in mountains” (Heb 11:38).
usage: “What doest thou here, Elijah?” (1Ki 19:9) — God's question to a man settled in his cave.
“was in the deserts till the day of his shewing unto Israel” (Luk 1:80) — a wilderness with a terminus.
“departed into a solitary place, and there prayed” (Mar 1:35) — the pattern: withdraw, pray, return.

pos: a. (of or belonging to hermits; the solitary form of monastic life, as opposed to cenobitic)
etymology: Greek eremites, a desert-dweller, from eremos, desert; the adjective of the solitary life.
biblical_def: Eremitic names the solitary form of the monastic life, in distinction from the cenobitic or communal form. The two have competed since the fourth century: Antony went alone into the Egyptian desert, Pachomius gathered men into a house, and every later rule had to decide which it preferred. Benedict ranked the cenobites first and allowed that a seasoned monk might afterwards go out alone; the Carthusians inverted it, building a community of solitaries. Scripture's weight falls plainly on the communal side. The church is a body whose members need each other — “And the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee: nor again the head to the feet, I have no need of you” (1Co 12:21) — and the duties the New Testament lays on Christians are nearly all reciprocal: bear one another's burdens, exhort one another, confess to one another. “Through desire a man, having separated himself, seeketh and intermeddleth with all wisdom” (Pro 18:1) puts separation under the heading of a man's own desire rather than of devotion, and the next verse makes the tone plain. The solitary may have a season; he cannot have a system, because a man alone cannot obey half of what he is commanded.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines eremite as a hermit, one who lives in a wilderness or in retirement; eremitical as living in solitude or retirement from society; and cenobite as one of a religious order living in a convent or in community.
webster_full: EREMITE, n. One who lives in a wilderness, or in retirement from society; a hermit.
EREMITICAL, a. Living in solitude or in retirement from the world; pertaining to a hermit.
CENOBITE, n. One of a religious order, living in a convent or in community, in opposition to an anchoret or hermit.
SOLITARY, a. Living alone; not having company; also, retired; remote from society; as a solitary residence.
COMMUNITY, n. A society of people having common rights and privileges, or common interests; a body of people united by some common bond.
scriptures: And the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee: nor again the head to the feet, I have no need of you.
Pro 18:1
Through desire a man, having separated himself, seeketh and intermeddleth with all wisdom.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
corruption_summary: The solitary monastic life: possible for a season, impossible as a system, since half the New Testament's commands require a brother to obey them with.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is structural. A life designed around solitude cannot obey the reciprocal commands, and those commands are not peripheral — “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another” (Heb 10:25) is addressed to the very temptation. A man who has arranged his life so that there is nobody to exhort him has not achieved a higher obedience; he has removed himself from the ordinary one.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the plain usefulness of company in the Christian life: “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour” (Ecc 4:9). Modern isolation is seldom chosen as devotion and is just as corrosive; the remedy in both cases is a congregation one is actually known in.
roots_summary: Greek eremos (G2048), desert; Greek koinonia (G2842), fellowship; Greek allelon (G240), one another; Hebrew badad (H909), alone; Greek episunagoge (G1997), an assembling together.
roots_lines: Greek eremos (G2048) — desert, solitary; the word the whole eremitic ideal is built on.
Greek koinonia (G2842) — fellowship, having in common; a New Testament mark of the church.
Greek allelon (G240) — one another; the pronoun of dozens of commands a solitary cannot keep.
Greek episunagoge (G1997) — a gathering together; “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25).
Hebrew badad (H909) — to be alone; “having separated himself” (Pro 18:1).
usage: “the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee” (1Co 12:21) — the body argument against a solitary system.
“Through desire a man, having separated himself” (Pro 18:1) — separation diagnosed, not praised.
“Two are better than one” (Ecc 4:9) — the plainest verdict in Scripture on the question.

pos: n. (an Eastern monastic settlement of separate cells grouped about a church; a colony of solitaries)
etymology: Greek laura, a lane or alley, perhaps from the passages between the cells; used in the East for a large monastery of semi-solitaries.
biblical_def: A lavra is an Eastern monastic settlement built as a cluster of separate cells about a common church: the monks lived alone through the week and gathered for the liturgy and a common meal, a middle path between the hermit and the house. The great lavras of Palestine — Mar Saba in the Kidron gorge, Euthymius in the Judean desert — shaped Eastern monasticism as Benedict shaped the West, and the Great Lavra on Mount Athos still gives the name to the senior houses there. The arrangement is the most defensible of the ascetic forms, because it keeps a congregation. A man who prays alone six days and communes with brethren on the seventh is at least within reach of what Scripture requires: “And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Act 2:42). The remaining objection is not solitude but geography: these settlements were placed in deserts specifically to be away from the people among whom the gospel must be preached and the poor must be fed, and a faith that withdraws to the Kidron cliffs has put a wilderness between itself and its neighbour.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines monastery as a house of religious retirement or of seclusion from the world; cell as a very small and close apartment, the hut of a hermit; and congregation as a collection or assembly of persons, particularly for divine worship.
webster_full: MONASTERY, n. A house of religious retirement, or of seclusion from ordinary temporal concerns, as an abbey, a priory, or a convent.
CELL, n. A very small and close apartment, as in a prison, or in a monastery or nunnery; the hut of a hermit.
CONGREGATION, n. A collection or assembly of separate things or persons; an assembly of persons met for the worship of God.
COLONY, n. A company of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country, and remaining subject to the jurisdiction of the parent state.
DESERT, n. An uninhabited tract of land; a region in its natural state; a wilderness; a solitude.
scriptures: Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
A Song of degrees of David. Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
Isa 58:7

Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?
corruption_summary: An Eastern colony of solitary cells about one church: the soundest of the ascetic forms, planted in a desert deliberately far from the neighbour it was to love.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the lavra's own best feature, which is that solitude is answerable to an assembly. “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!” (Psa 133:1) describes what the common church of a lavra at least attempted.

The live defect is distance from the neighbour. Love of neighbour is not an abstraction in Scripture but a matter of bread and lodging — “Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house?” (Isa 58:7) — and a settlement sited to be unreachable has made that obedience impossible by design, however earnest its prayers.
roots_summary: Greek laura, a lane; Greek koinonia (G2842), fellowship; Hebrew midbar (H4057), wilderness; Hebrew yachad (H3162), together; Greek ekklesia (G1577), an assembly.
roots_lines: Greek laura — a lane or passage; the settlements were named for the alleys between their cells.
Greek ekklesia (G1577) — an assembly called out; what the common church of a lavra was reaching for.
Hebrew yachad (H3162) — together, in union; “for brethren to dwell together in unity” (Psa 133:1).
Hebrew midbar (H4057) — wilderness; the deliberate setting of the Palestinian lavras.
Greek koinonia (G2842) — fellowship; “in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship” (Act 2:42).
usage: “in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Act 2:42) — the common life a lavra kept weekly.
“how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together” (Psa 133:1) — the warrant for the common church.
“Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry” (Isa 58:7) — the obedience a desert address forecloses.

pos: n. (one who scourges himself as penance; a member of the public self-whipping processions of 1260 and 1349)
etymology: Latin flagellare, to whip, from flagellum, a whip or scourge; the flagellant is one who applies it to himself.
biblical_def: The flagellants were men who scourged themselves as penance, and in two great outbreaks — Italy in 1260, and across Germany and the Low Countries during the Black Death of 1349 — they moved in public processions, stripped to the waist, whipping themselves through the streets and calling the towns to repent. The movement was condemned by the papacy in 1349 and became openly heretical in places, claiming that its own blood atoned. Scripture leaves no room for the practice at all. Self-cutting as religion is the mark of the prophets of Baal on Carmel: “And they cried aloud, and cut themselves after their manner with knives and lancets, till the blood gushed out upon them” (1Ki 18:28). It is forbidden to Israel by name — “Ye shall not make any cuttings in your flesh for the dead, nor print any marks upon you: I am the LORD” (Lev 19:28) and “ye shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead” (Deu 14:1). And the blood that atones is not the penitent's. Where a flagellant believed his stripes availed for sin, the answer is the stripes of another: “he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities” (Isa 53:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines flagellant as one who whips himself in religious discipline; flagellation as a beating or whipping, a flogging; and scourge as a whip, a lash, and figuratively a punishment or a means of inflicting punishment.
webster_full: FLAGELLANT, n. One who whips himself in religious discipline; a name given to fanatics who made public processions, lashing themselves.
FLAGELLATION, n. A beating or whipping; a flogging; the act of scourging, particularly as a religious discipline.
SCOURGE, n. A whip; a lash consisting of a strap or cord; an instrument of punishment or discipline.
PENANCE, n. The suffering, labor or pain to which a person voluntarily subjects himself, or which is imposed on him by authority as a punishment for his sins.
ATONEMENT, n. Expiation; satisfaction or reparation made by giving an equivalent for an injury, or by doing or suffering that which is received in satisfaction for an offense.
scriptures: And they cried aloud, and cut themselves after their manner with knives and lancets, till the blood gushed out upon them.
Ye shall not make any cuttings in your flesh for the dead, nor print any marks upon you: I am the LORD.
Deu 14:1
Ye are the children of the LORD your God: ye shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead.
Isa 53:5
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
corruption_summary: Public self-scourging as penance: a practice Scripture assigns to the prophets of Baal, forbidding it by name, and answered by the stripes of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is as grave as any in this dictionary, because it touches the atonement. A man who bleeds to pay for sin is denying that the payment has been made, and Scripture sets the two bloods side by side without comment because none is needed: Baal's prophets “cut themselves after their manner with knives and lancets” (1Ki 18:28), while of Christ it is written “and with his stripes we are healed” (Isa 53:5). One of those is a gospel and the other is not.

The modern form is self-harm, which is usually grief rather than religion and must be met with compassion rather than a sermon — but the theology beneath the medieval version is also alive wherever Christians punish themselves to feel forgiven. The principle to recover is that repentance is inward and the satisfaction is Christ's: “And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God: for he is gracious and merciful” (Joe 2:13).
roots_summary: Latin flagellum, a whip; Hebrew gadad (H1413), to cut oneself; Greek mastix (G3148), a scourge; Hebrew chabburah (H2250), a stripe or bruise; Greek hilasmos (G2434), propitiation.
roots_lines: Latin flagellum — a whip or scourge; the instrument that names the movement.
Hebrew gadad (H1413) — to cut or gash oneself; the verb of Carmel and of the pagan mourning rites.
Hebrew chabburah (H2250) — a stripe, a bruise; “with his stripes we are healed” (Isa 53:5).
Greek mastix (G3148) — a scourge; “and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth” (Heb 12:6) — God's hand, not the penitent's.
Greek hilasmos (G2434) — propitiation; what Christ is, and what no self-inflicted blood can supply.
usage: “Ye shall not make any cuttings in your flesh” (Lev 19:28) — the practice forbidden by name.
“till the blood gushed out upon them” (1Ki 18:28) — the company self-scourging keeps in Scripture.
“rend your heart, and not your garments” (Joe 2:13) — the repentance God asks instead.

pos: n. (a garment of coarse animal hair worn next to the skin as penance; the cilice)
etymology: From hair and shirt; rendering Latin cilicium, cloth of Cilician goat hair, the material of ancient sackcloth.
biblical_def: A hair shirt is a garment of coarse goat or horse hair worn against the skin to irritate it continually, a standard instrument of medieval penance worn under the ordinary habit and so invisible. The material has a biblical history, since the cilicium of coarse hair is precisely the sackcloth of Scripture, and sackcloth is a real and approved sign of mourning and repentance: it is worn at the news of disaster, in national humiliation, and by prophets. The difference between sackcloth and a hair shirt is the difference between a sign and a mechanism. Sackcloth announced a grief already felt, for a season, publicly. A hair shirt is worn permanently and secretly to generate suffering that is then credited as penance, and that is the error God himself dismantles in Isaiah: “Is it such a fast that I have chosen? a day for a man to afflict his soul? is it to bow down his head as a bulrush, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him?” (Isa 58:5). The fast he does choose follows immediately, and it has nothing to do with the wearer's skin: “to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free” (Isa 58:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hair cloth as stuff or cloth made of hair, or in part with hair; sackcloth as cloth of which sacks are made, coarse cloth worn in mourning; and penance as suffering voluntarily undergone as a punishment for sin.
webster_full: HAIRCLOTH, n. Stuff or cloth made of hair, or in part with hair; used for various purposes.
SACKCLOTH, n. Cloth of which sacks are made; coarse cloth. This was formerly worn in mourning and in token of humiliation.
CILICE, n. A hair cloth; a garment of hair worn next the skin as a penance.
PENANCE, n. The suffering, labor or pain to which a person voluntarily subjects himself, or which is imposed on him by authority as a punishment for his sins.
MORTIFY, v.t. To subdue or bring into subjection, as the appetites and passions, by abstinence or rigorous severities.
scriptures: Isa 58:5

Is it such a fast that I have chosen? a day for a man to afflict his soul? is it to bow down his head as a bulrush, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? wilt thou call this a fast, and an acceptable day to the LORD?
Isa 58:6
Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?
Joe 2:13
And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God: for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil.
Col 2:23
Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.
corruption_summary: Coarse hair worn against the skin as penance: sackcloth was a sign of grief, a hair shirt a mechanism for producing it, and God rejects the second in Isaiah by name.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the conversion of a sign into a machine. Paul's category for it is exact: a practice with “a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh” (Col 2:23). The last clause is the sting — such severity does not actually subdue the flesh, it feeds the pride of the man who sustains it, which is why the secret hair shirt was so easily boasted of after death.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Isaiah's own substitution. God answers a nation's self-affliction by redirecting it to the oppressed and the hungry: “and that ye break every yoke?” (Isa 58:6). A Christian who wants to mortify the flesh will find more of it dying over a neighbour's burden than under any garment.
roots_summary: Latin cilicium, Cilician hair cloth; Hebrew saq (H8242), sackcloth; Hebrew anah (H6031), to afflict; Greek sakkos (G4526), sackcloth; Greek apheidia from pheidomai (G5339), unsparing severity.
roots_lines: Latin cilicium — cloth of Cilician goat hair; the material of sackcloth and of the hair shirt alike.
Hebrew saq (H8242) — sackcloth; a sign of mourning worn openly and for a season.
Hebrew anah (H6031) — to afflict, to humble; “a day for a man to afflict his soul” (Isa 58:5).
Greek sakkos (G4526) — sackcloth; retained in the New Testament as a sign of repentance, never as a merit.
Greek pheidomai (G5339) — to spare; its negation is the “neglecting of the body” Paul rejects.
usage: “Is it such a fast that I have chosen?” (Isa 58:5) — God's own question about self-affliction.
“to let the oppressed go free” (Isa 58:6) — the fast he does choose.
“not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh” (Col 2:23) — why the severity fails on its own terms.

pos: n. (the putting to death of sinful desire; in medieval usage, bodily austerities undertaken to that end)
etymology: Latin mortificare, to put to death, from mors, death, and facere, to make; with caro, flesh.
biblical_def: Mortification of the flesh is a genuinely biblical duty which medieval practice badly misdirected, and the whole question turns on what flesh means. In Paul it is not the body but fallen nature — the self in rebellion — and what is to be killed is named: “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry” (Col 3:5). The agent is the Spirit, not the whip: “if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live” (Rom 8:13). And it is spoken of as already accomplished in principle: “And they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts” (Gal 5:24). Paul does discipline his body — “But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection” (1Co 9:27) — so bodily discipline is not foreign to the duty. But he treats the body as a servant to be trained, never as an enemy to be punished, and he sets a firm limit on what such training can achieve: “For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things” (1Ti 4:8). Medieval austerity attacked the body and left the covetousness untouched.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mortification as the act of subduing the passions and appetites by penance, abstinence or painful severities inflicted on the body; mortify as to subdue inordinate passions; and flesh as the body, and in a scriptural sense human nature in its corrupt state.
webster_full: MORTIFICATION, n. The act of subduing the passions and appetites by penance, abstinence or painful severities inflicted on the body.
MORTIFY, v.t. To subdue or bring into subjection, as the appetites and passions; to abase, as pride.
FLESH, n. In a scriptural sense, human nature in its corrupt state, or the carnal appetites and affections; as, the works of the flesh.
SUBDUE, v.t. To conquer by force or the exertion of superior power, and bring into permanent subjection; to tame.
CONCUPISCENCE, n. Lust; unlawful or irregular desire of sexual pleasure; inordinate desire.
scriptures: Col 3:5
Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry:
Rom 8:13
For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live.
Gal 5:24
And they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts.
But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.
corruption_summary: Putting sinful desire to death: a real command aimed at covetousness and lust, which medieval practice redirected onto the body itself.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is a mistranslation lived out. Reading flesh as the body produces an attack on skin, sleep and food, while the sins Paul actually lists — covetousness above all — survive untouched and even flourish in a man proud of his austerities. Paul foresaw the outcome: such rigour is “not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh” (Col 2:23), which is to say it does not even achieve what it is for.

The modern inversion denies the duty altogether, treating desire as identity and mortification as self-hatred. That is worse, not better. The principle to recover is the true target and the true agent: “if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live” (Rom 8:13) — and the first thing on the list to die is “covetousness, which is idolatry” (Col 3:5), which no hair shirt has ever reached.
roots_summary: Latin mortificare, to put to death; Greek nekroo (G3499), to make dead; Greek thanatoo (G2289), to put to death; Greek sarx (G4561), flesh; Greek doulagogeo (G1396), to bring into subjection.
roots_lines: Greek nekroo (G3499) — to make dead; “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth” (Col 3:5).
Greek thanatoo (G2289) — to put to death; the verb of “do mortify the deeds of the body” (Rom 8:13).
Greek sarx (G4561) — flesh; in Paul the fallen nature, not the physical frame.
Greek doulagogeo (G1396) — to lead as a slave, to bring under; “But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection” (1Co 9:27).
Greek epithumia (G1939) — lust, strong desire; “have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts” (Gal 5:24).
usage: “covetousness, which is idolatry” (Col 3:5) — the sin at the head of the list, untouched by austerity.
“if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body” (Rom 8:13) — the Spirit, not the scourge.
“For bodily exercise profiteth little” (1Ti 4:8) — the proportion medieval practice reversed.

pos: n. pl. (the Second Order of St Francis, the enclosed sisters founded by Clare of Assisi in 1212)
etymology: From Clare (Italian Chiara) of Assisi, with poor rendering the order's title, the Order of Poor Ladies.
biblical_def: The Poor Clares are the Second Order of the Franciscan family: enclosed sisters founded at San Damiano in 1212 by Clare of Assisi, who fought the papal curia for forty years to keep her house as poor as Francis's friars and won her rule two days before she died. Their life was strict enclosure, manual work, and absolute poverty, and Clare's tenacity about the last of these is genuinely impressive: she would not accept the endowments successive popes pressed on her, because an endowed house is a secure house and she had read the gospel otherwise. The honest Protestant judgment is the one already given of the whole mendicant ideal. “Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom” (Jam 2:5) speaks of God's election of the actually poor, not of a voluntary destitution that earns. And enclosure cuts a Christian woman off from the very duties Scripture names as hers: “That they may teach the young women to be sober, to love their husbands, to love their children” (Tit 2:4), and “if she have lodged strangers, if she have washed the saints' feet, if she have relieved the afflicted” (1Ti 5:10). A wall makes those commands unperformable.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines nun as a woman devoted to a religious life who lives in a convent under vows; convent as a house for persons devoted to religion; and cloister as a place of religious retirement, a monastery or nunnery.
webster_full: NUN, n. A woman devoted to a religious life, who lives in a cloister or nunnery, under vows of chastity, poverty and obedience.
NUNNERY, n. A house in which nuns reside; a cloister in which females live sequestered from the world.
CONVENT, n. A house for persons devoted to religion; an abbey; a monastery; a nunnery.
CLOISTER, n. A monastery or nunnery; a house inhabited by monks or nuns; also, a place of religious retirement.
POOR, a. Wholly destitute of property, or not having property sufficient for a comfortable subsistence.
scriptures: Jam 2:5
Hearken, my beloved brethren, Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he hath promised to them that love him?
Tit 2:4
That they may teach the young women to be sober, to love their husbands, to love their children,

Well reported of for good works; if she have brought up children, if she have lodged strangers, if she have washed the saints' feet, if she have relieved the afflicted, if she have diligently followed every good work.
She stretcheth out her hand to the poor; yea, she reacheth forth her hands to the needy.
corruption_summary: The enclosed Franciscan sisters: Clare's refusal of endowment was courage, and the wall she accepted made the duties Scripture gives a woman unperformable.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is twofold, and the second half is the heavier. Vowed poverty as merit has been treated already. Enclosure is the sharper problem, because Scripture's charge to Christian women is unmistakably relational and material — teaching younger women, lodging strangers, relieving the afflicted, reaching the needy — and a grille forbids all of it. “She stretcheth out her hand to the poor; yea, she reacheth forth her hands to the needy” (Pro 31:20) is not a figure of speech.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour Scripture already places on the ordinary Christian woman's life. The medieval church offered its most devout daughters a wall because it had no higher category for a wife and mother; Scripture has no higher category because it needs none.
roots_summary: Greek ptochos (G4434), poor; Greek parthenos (G3933), a virgin; Hebrew chayil (H2428), strength or virtue; Greek oikodespoteo (G3616), to rule a household; Greek philoxenia (G5381), hospitality.
roots_lines: Greek ptochos (G4434) — the destitute poor; “Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith” (Jam 2:5).
Hebrew chayil (H2428) — strength, ability, worth; the word behind the virtuous woman of Proverbs 31.
Greek philoxenia (G5381) — love of strangers, hospitality; “if she have lodged strangers” (1Ti 5:10).
Greek oikodespoteo (G3616) — to manage a household; a charge Paul gives to younger women.
Greek parthenos (G3933) — a virgin; a real condition in Scripture, never a rank.
usage: “That they may teach the young women to be sober” (Tit 2:4) — a duty a grille forbids.
“She stretcheth out her hand to the poor” (Pro 31:20) — the reach enclosure prevents.
“rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom” (Jam 2:5) — God's choice of the poor, not poverty's purchase.

pos: n. (in canon law, the rule confining members of a religious house within its walls; strictest for women, where it was papally imposed)
etymology: Latin inclusura, a shutting in, from includere, to shut in; the same word that in English history names the fencing of common land.
biblical_def: Enclosure is the canonical rule confining the members of a religious house within its precinct. For monks it was moderate; for women it hardened steadily, until Boniface VIII in 1298 and then the Council of Trent imposed strict papal enclosure on every community of nuns, so that a professed woman might not leave her convent for life and visitors spoke to her through a grille. The motives mixed real concern for safety with a low estimate of what a woman could be trusted to do unsupervised. Scripture's own direction for the church is the reverse of a wall. Christ's prayer is explicit: “I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil” (Joh 17:15), and “As thou hast sent me into the world, even so have I also sent them into the world” (Joh 17:18). His image for a disciple is a lamp placed where it can be seen: “Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house” (Mat 5:15). Paul had to correct the Corinthians for reading his discipline as withdrawal, remarking that to avoid every sinner “then must ye needs go out of the world” (1Co 5:10) — which is exactly what enclosure attempted.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines enclosure as the act of enclosing, the separation of land from common ground by a fence, and that which is enclosed; cloister as a place of religious retirement; and grate as a partition or frame of cross bars.
webster_full: ENCLOSURE, n. The act of enclosing or separating from common grounds by a fence; also, the appropriation of things common; and the space enclosed.
ENCLOSE, v.t. To surround; to shut up; to encompass; to confine on all sides; to shut in.
CLOISTER, n. A monastery or nunnery; a house inhabited by monks or nuns; a place of religious retirement.
GRATE, n. A partition made with bars placed near each other, or crossing each other, as the grate of a prison or cloister.
SECLUSION, n. The act of separating from society or connection; the state of being separate or apart; retirement; privacy; solitude.
scriptures: I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil.
As thou hast sent me into the world, even so have I also sent them into the world.
Mat 5:15
Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house.
Yet not altogether with the fornicators of this world, or with the covetous, or extortioners, or with idolaters; for then must ye needs go out of the world.
corruption_summary: The rule that walled a religious house in, strictest for women: safety and suspicion together, against a Lord who prayed his people be kept in the world and not taken out of it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the removal of Christians from the world Christ sent them into, and it falls hardest on women. A professed woman under strict enclosure could not teach a young wife, lodge a stranger, visit the sick or reach the needy — all duties Scripture names as hers — and “She stretcheth out her hand to the poor; yea, she reacheth forth her hands to the needy” (Pro 31:20) becomes unperformable behind a grille. A rule that makes obedience impossible is not a stricter obedience.

The second corruption is the estimate of women underneath it. Scripture gives a Christian woman a demanding and public-facing charge — “I will therefore that the younger women marry, bear children, guide the house” (1Ti 5:14), and “To be discreet, chaste, keepers at home, good, obedient to their own husbands” (Tit 2:5) — which honours the household as the sphere of real labour and real authority. The principle to recover is that light is for a candlestick: “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven” (Mat 5:16).
roots_summary: Latin includere, to shut in; Greek kosmos (G2889), the world; Greek apostello (G649), to send out; Greek luchnia (G3087), a candlestick; Hebrew gader (H1447), a wall or fence.
roots_lines: Latin inclusura — a shutting in; the same root as the inclusus, a man walled into a cell.
Greek kosmos (G2889) — the world; “I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world” (Joh 17:15).
Greek apostello (G649) — to send forth; “even so have I also sent them into the world” (Joh 17:18).
Greek luchnia (G3087) — a candlestick or lampstand; “but on a candlestick” (Mat 5:15).
Hebrew gader (H1447) — a wall or hedge; in Scripture a protection of a vineyard, not of a soul.
usage: “As thou hast sent me into the world, even so have I also sent them into the world” (Joh 17:18) — the commission a wall contradicts.
“put it under a bushel” (Mat 5:15) — Christ's own figure for hidden light.
“then must ye needs go out of the world” (1Co 5:10) — Paul naming the absurdity of total withdrawal.
